title: Bud Powell and Fats Navarro sessions for Savoy
summary: Hall made some of the first bebop records on gigs arranged by Walter Fuller, without feeling they were historic.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Yeah, I know. We are going to get into that but what I was interested in was the period in New York from say, '39 to '45 because this is a period in which bebop or modern jazz, whatever, came up, and you know, the sessions uptown which have been written about so much and talked about started around you know, '39 or '41, I guess and then you know, Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, The- lonious Monk, this was all happening in this same period and during the war.
Well, I made the first bebop records for Savoy with Bud Powell and --
Yeah, you and Sonny Stitt and
Yeah, Sonny Stitt and some with Benny [HARRIS] and Fats Navarro.
Now, how did this come about?
They were just gigs. We are looking at it in retrospect, but they were just gigs then, you know. I got called, Walter Fuller was the arranger, a friend
of mine, and --
That's how you happened to get called.
Yeah, I guess so.
Where do you know Walter from?
Just around. We were all aspiring, struggling persons.
Yeah, but you had already worked with Teddy and Ellis, because this is 1945, '45 and '46 around there.
Yeah, but it didn't mean that much financially.
I'm not talking about it from that standpoint.
We didn't look at it in terms of whether this is the start of -- (jazz)
No, no. You were an established bassist you know --
I was established, I'd been established since I'd been here.

Yeah, so, I'm not talking about from the standpoint of big bucks or stardom or anything, I'm talking about just from the musical standpoint. Now, you had heard the music, you had been here so you had heard the different changes taking place.
Yeah.
How did this hit you?
I just went along with what I had been to doing.
No, I mean before you made those dates, I'm saying, you heard the new, what was your reaction to --
I didn't have any reaction to it.
Did you feel it was a natural continuation?
Yeah. My Wax Records, which I got accolades for --
I told you I was one of your record buyers.
Was one of the last of that type of music because now the guys would come home from the war with a different sound.
Well, a lot of people that were away didn't even hear it, you know, all of a sudden they came back and that's why, it was a shock to a lot of people because they hadn't heard it happening.
Right.
They thought it, you know, here it is.
